analysis.title: The High Cost Of Cheap Intelligence: AI Is Deflating 13x A Year, Faster Than Any Technology In History
key_insights: Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid, citing Epoch AI, says the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% a quarter, or 13x a year, since 2023. That is 4x faster than DNA sequencing, 6x faster than compute and 18x faster than lithium batteries.

On the chart's log scale, electricity took eight decades to fall to roughly 2% of its starting cost and compute took 60 years to fall eleven orders of magnitude. AI fell roughly five orders of magnitude in about five years (ZeroHedge's reading off the chart, approximate).

Reid says even the most enthusiastic estimates put the industry about three orders of magnitude (1,000x) short of the computing power needed for AGI. ZeroHedge's own arithmetic: at 13x a year, a 1,000x gap closes in under three years, which is why the 'San Francisco Consensus' pencilled in superintelligence by 2030.

The cost decline is being driven by capex. US and Chinese hyperscalers and neoclouds are set to invest almost $1 trillion this year on AI-related capex, almost twice last year's level, and Reid expects it to be exceeded again in each of the next few years.

ZeroHedge's revenue math: if the price of a unit of AI output falls 13x a year, volumes must rise 13x a year just to keep revenue flat, and demand must grow faster still to justify capex that doubled in a year.

Reid says the deflation story only works if enterprises see growing returns on their AI spend (employee productivity, more efficient workflows, new products and services). The report invokes Solow's paradox and the productivity J-curve, and is not optimistic on timing.

Funding is shifting from free cash flow to debt. Morgan Stanley warns AI's $1.6 trillion capex plan lives or dies in the credit market (Oct 19), and ZeroHedge notes there have been zero hyperscaler/AI investment-grade debt deals since the start of September, with SPVs doing no better.

Goldman (Sep 25) estimated the revenue needed to justify $1.7 trillion in hyperscaler capex and found it well above what is currently showing up. Goldman also said token demand growth must outpace declining token prices, and hyperscaler ROIC has slid to record lows (per ZeroHedge).

ZeroHedge's take: a product that loses 92% of its value a year (47% a quarter compounded) is a treadmill for the hyperscalers, who must sell 13x more intelligence each year to stand still while spending twice as much and increasingly borrowing. They plan to revisit when hyperscalers report later this month and update capex guidance.

sector_views.rationale: Falling AI costs benefit users, but hyperscalers must grow volumes 13x a year to hold revenue flat while capex roughly doubled to almost $1T and funding shifts to debt.

earnings_insights: Hyperscaler earnings are expected later in October 2026, with updated capex guidance the item ZeroHedge says it will check.
risk_factors: Hyperscalers may be unable to earn a return on roughly $1T of annual AI capex if token prices keep falling 13x a year.
Credit market access: no hyperscaler/AI IG debt deals since the start of September, and SPVs are not doing better.
Enterprises may not turn AI spend into measurable productivity soon enough (Solow's paradox, J-curve timing).
Jevons-effect demand gains may mostly benefit cheap Chinese models rather than US hyperscalers (per a ZeroHedge post).
Extrapolating the cost curve to AGI by 2030 may not hold.

tension_points.theme: AI cost deflation vs capex return
tension_points.bull_case: AI costs falling 13x a year benefit users and could close the 1,000x compute gap to AGI in under three years, if scaling keeps delivering.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscalers must sell 13x more volume a year to keep revenue flat while capex roughly doubled to almost $1T and is increasingly debt-funded, with no IG deals since September and ROIC at record lows.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Enterprises fail to show measurable productivity gains from AI spend, or the credit market stays shut to hyperscaler debt.
